annotations.keyFindings: Direct cessation shortened time on high flow (median 26 against 44 hours) and length of stay by 18 hours; re-escalation 11 against 8 percent, compatible with chance.
annotations.limitations: Only 21 percent of infants were younger than 3 months; imprecise for rare harms.

annotations.keyFindings: In infants younger than 8 weeks, re-escalation within 48 hours was 24 percent after abrupt discontinuation against 12 percent after stepwise weaning; no difference in older infants.
annotations.limitations: Practice chosen by ward; wards using abrupt discontinuation admitted younger, sicker infants.

annotations.keyFindings: A nurse-driven weaning protocol in three PDSA cycles was followed by median time on high flow falling from 49 to 30 hours; adherence was 62 percent at night against 85 percent by day.
annotations.limitations: Single ward, one season, no concurrent comparison.

annotations.keyFindings: In 2,410 episodes, re-escalation within 24 hours did not differ between direct cessation and stepwise weaning, including in infants younger than 8 weeks (13.1 against 12.4 percent).
annotations.limitations: Not peer reviewed; no posting year; adjustment variables limited to age, oxygen and hospital.
annotations.notes: No grade or quality score assigned: unreviewed methods and no posting year.

annotations.keyFindings: Parents found long weaning confusing and wanted to know the criteria for stopping and restarting high flow.
annotations.limitations: Two wards; conversations held on the ward.

annotations.keyFindings: Scheduled respiratory assessments were missed in 18 percent of night hours against 6 percent of day hours, most often between 02:00 and 05:00.
Weaning practice varied widely and only 18 percent of hospitalists had a written weaning protocol.

claims.text: In a trial of 184 infants, direct cessation of high flow after two stable hours shortened time on high flow without a clear increase in re-escalation.
claims.passage: Time on high flow was shorter with direct cessation (median 26 against 44 hours)
claims.interpretation: Supports the direct-cessation protocol for most infants; few very young infants were included.

claims.text: A ward weaning protocol tested in PDSA cycles was followed by a fall in median time on high flow from 49 to 30 hours, with lower adherence at night.
claims.passage: Median time on high flow fell from 49 to 30 hours on the run chart
claims.interpretation: The change can be tested and tracked on a single ward in one season; night delivery is the weak point.

claims.text: Whether direct cessation increases re-escalation in infants younger than 8 weeks is unresolved: one observational study found twice the re-escalation, and an undated, unreviewed analysis found no difference.
claims.passage: Among infants younger than 8 weeks, re-escalation within 48 hours occurred in 24 percent after abrupt discontinuation and 12 percent after stepwise weaning
claims.interpretation: Conflicting and confounded evidence; keep stepwise weaning for infants under 8 weeks until local data exist.

claims.text: Scheduled respiratory assessments were missed in 18 percent of night hours on pediatric wards.
claims.passage: Scheduled assessments were missed in 18 percent of night hours and 6 percent of day hours.
claims.interpretation: Two-hourly checks at night need a realistic schedule and a process measure.

claims.text: Parents wanted to be told the criteria for stopping and restarting high flow.
claims.passage: Parents wanted to be told the criteria for stopping and restarting high flow.
claims.interpretation: Share the protocol's criteria with parents at the bedside.

synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. A trial and a ward improvement report agree that direct cessation after a short stable period shortens time on high flow by roughly 18 to 20 hours without a clear rise in re-escalation. For infants younger than 8 weeks the evidence conflicts: a confounded observational study found re-escalation doubled after abrupt discontinuation, while an undated preprint found no difference; neither settles the question. Night assessments are often missed, and parents want clear criteria. The evidence supports testing the protocol locally for infants aged 8 weeks or older with close safety monitoring.
gradeRationale: One small trial with few young infants, one improvement report and conflicting observational evidence for the youngest infants; low certainty overall, very uncertain for infants under 8 weeks.
summary: Seven retrieved records appraised; five claims recorded, one of them with high uncertainty because the evidence conflicts.
